Data & performance::Artifacts.summary: Artifacts store files produced by a GitHub Actions workflow so they survive a job and can be shared with another job in the same run. They are useful for build output, logs, binaries, and other files needed after the run.
Data & performance::Artifacts.explanation: An artifact is a file or group of files created during a workflow run. Upload it before the producing job ends, then download it by name in another job from the same run; the stored artifact remains available after the run for later access.
Data & performance::Artifacts.syntax:
uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
with:
  name: artifact-name
  path: path/to/files

uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
with:
  name: artifact-name
  path: destination

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Artifact name used to identify the uploaded or downloaded files.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Files or directories to upload with upload-artifact.

parameters.name: retention-days
parameters.description: Number of days to retain an uploaded artifact.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Directory where download-artifact places downloaded files.

Data & performance::Artifacts.returns: Uploaded files are stored as a named artifact and can later be downloaded or deleted; downloaded files are placed in the workspace by default.

example.title: Pass build output between jobs
example.code:
name: Build and test
on: push
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: mkdir -p dist && echo "build output" > dist/app.txt
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: build-output
          path: dist
  test:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: build-output
      - run: cat dist/app.txt
example.explanation: The first job uploads files under a named artifact before it ends. The dependent job downloads that artifact from the same workflow run and can then use the files in its workspace.

useCases.title: Transfer build output
useCases.scenario: A compile job produces binaries that a packaging or deployment job needs.

useCases.title: Retain diagnostics
useCases.scenario: A workflow generates test reports, logs, or screenshots that developers must inspect after completion.

useCases.title: Access post-run files
useCases.scenario: A completed run's generated files need to be downloaded or managed later through GitHub or the REST API.

interview.question: How do you pass build output from one job to another?
interview.answer: Upload the files with the upload-artifact action before the producing job finishes, assigning the artifact a name. A later job can use download-artifact with that name, provided both jobs belong to the same workflow run.
interview.followUp: How would you choose between artifacts and dependency caching? Use artifacts for files produced by a job that must be viewed after the run or passed between jobs; use caching for reusable dependencies.

interview.question: How can you control how long an artifact remains available?
interview.answer: The artifact is stored beyond the producing job and can be accessed after the workflow completes. Its retention can be customized for an individual artifact with the retention-days input on upload-artifact.
interview.followUp: What happens if the workflow run is deleted? All artifacts associated with that run are deleted from storage.

interview.question: When should artifacts be used instead of caching or job outputs?
interview.answer: Artifacts are appropriate for build binaries, logs, test output, and other files produced by a workflow. They differ from step-to-step data passing: steps in one job share a runner environment, while separate jobs need artifacts to transfer files.
interview.followUp: What is the simpler mechanism for passing values between steps in one job? Use inputs and outputs rather than an artifact.

keyPoints: Artifacts package files generated by a workflow run so they can be transferred or retained.
Use artifacts both to preserve job output and to make it available to another job.
The producing job must assign a name and upload its files before it finishes.
The consuming job identifies the desired artifact by its assigned name.
Completed-run artifacts remain manageable through GitHub or the REST API.
Choose artifacts for output that must be inspected or used after the workflow ends.
gotchas: A job cannot download an artifact from a different workflow run.
Artifacts have a default retention period of 90 days in the documented GitHub Enterprise Server context; configure a custom period when needed.
Deleting the workflow run also removes its associated artifacts.

Data & performance::Concurrency groups.sourceTitle: Control the concurrency of workflows and jobs
Data & performance::Concurrency groups.summary: Concurrency groups limit a workflow or job to one active run for a shared key. Add `cancel-in-progress: true` to stop the older run when a newer run uses the same key.
Data & performance::Concurrency groups.explanation: A concurrency group is a shared key attached at workflow or job scope. GitHub permits one active item for a key; later items wait, and cancel-in-progress can terminate the active item so the newer run proceeds. The key may be fixed or computed from supported contexts.

parameters.name: group
parameters.description: A string or supported expression identifying the shared concurrency group.

parameters.name: cancel-in-progress
parameters.description: Whether to cancel the currently running job or workflow in the same group; may be true, false, or an expression.

example.title: Cancel superseded branch runs
example.code:
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
example.explanation: This workflow gives each workflow-and-branch pair its own group and cancels an older in-progress run when a newer run enters that group.

useCases.title: Keep only the latest branch validation
useCases.scenario: A branch receives several pushes while CI is running.

useCases.title: Serialize deployments
useCases.scenario: A deployment target must not receive overlapping releases.

useCases.title: Protect a shared test resource
useCases.scenario: A shared external resource supports one test session at a time.

interview.question: What does a concurrency group control?
interview.answer: Concurrency groups serialize workflow runs or jobs that resolve to the same key. Define `concurrency` at workflow scope to coordinate whole runs, or under a job to coordinate only that job.
interview.followUp: How would you prevent two branches from canceling each other? Include a branch or ref component in the group expression so each branch resolves to a distinct key.

interview.question: How do you cancel superseded runs?
interview.answer: Set `cancel-in-progress: true` alongside the group. A newer run then cancels the currently running item with the same key instead of leaving it active while the newer run waits.
interview.followUp: When should cancellation be conditional? Use an expression when only selected events, branches, or environments should cancel active work.

interview.question: What values can form a concurrency key?
interview.answer: The group can be a literal string or an expression. Supported contexts include `github`, `inputs`, `vars`, `needs`, `strategy`, and `matrix`, so the key can reflect workflow, event, inputs, or matrix data.
interview.followUp: What design concern follows from dynamic keys? Ensure equivalent resources produce exactly the same key and unrelated resources do not collide.

keyPoints: Attach concurrency to a job when only one instance of that job should occupy a shared resource.
Use a constant for one global lock or interpolate context values to create separate locks.
Dynamic group expressions may read these contexts when deriving the key.
The cancellation switch changes a waiting newcomer into a replacement for the active group member.
Workflow-level configuration coordinates complete workflow runs rather than an individual job.
The key is the declaration that assigns work to a concurrency namespace.
gotchas: Cancellation applies only when the incoming run uses the identical resolved group key; choose the expression carefully to avoid canceling unrelated branches or workflows.

Data & performance::Dependency caching.summary: GitHub Actions dependency caching restores files using a key and can save them automatically when no exact cache exists. Hashing a lockfile into the key ties cache reuse to the dependency set.
Data & performance::Dependency caching.explanation: The cache action stores the directory specified by path under a key. A lockfile hash makes the key change when dependency declarations change; restoration first tries an exact key, then partial matches and optional restore keys. If nothing exact matches, a successful job automatically saves the specified files under the new key.
Data & performance::Dependency caching.syntax:
uses: actions/cache@v4
with:
  path: <directory>
  key: <cache-key>
  restore-keys: <optional-prefixes>

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Files or directories to restore and save.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The cache identifier used for lookup and saving; it can combine variables, contexts, strings, and functions.

parameters.name: restore-keys
parameters.description: Optional prefixes checked sequentially for partial matches when the primary key has no match.

Data & performance::Dependency caching.returns: Restores matching cached files to path; on a miss, saves path under key after a successful job.

example.title: Cache npm dependencies
example.code:
name: Cache dependencies
on: push
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Cache npm
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: ~/.npm
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-npm-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-npm-
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
example.explanation: This workflow caches npm's package cache using an operating-system prefix and a hash of package-lock.json, then restores a prior prefix match when no exact key exists.

useCases.title: Reuse npm download data between builds
useCases.scenario: JavaScript or TypeScript CI

useCases.title: Invalidate caches when a lockfile changes
useCases.scenario: Dependency updates

useCases.title: Keep operating-system caches separate
useCases.scenario: Multiple runner platforms

useCases.title: Fall back to a compatible partial cache
useCases.scenario: Cold or changed dependency sets

interview.question: How would you design a dependency-cache key?
interview.answer: The key identifies a cache version. Include a platform component and a hash of the dependency lockfile so caches are separated by runner environment and invalidated when dependencies change. The path tells the action which files to restore and save.
interview.followUp: Why add restore-keys? They allow a partial match when the exact lockfile key is absent. The most recent matching cache can reduce download work, but dependency installation must refresh it as needed.

interview.question: Describe the cache lookup order.
interview.answer: The action first looks for an exact key, then partial matches of that key, and finally the supplied restore keys in sequence. An exact match is a hit; otherwise the result is a miss.
interview.followUp: What happens after a miss? If the job succeeds, the action automatically creates a cache using the requested key and path contents.

interview.question: How does the example cache npm dependencies safely?
interview.answer: Use the cache action with a path, key, and optionally restore-keys. The example hashes package-lock.json and caches ~/.npm, then runs npm ci so the workflow remains correct even when a fallback cache is restored.
interview.followUp: Why not cache node_modules directly? The documented mechanism caches whichever path is selected; a package-manager cache is generally more portable across runner environments and installs.

keyPoints: Restoration has an ordered lookup process: exact key, partial key matches, then restore-key prefixes.
An exact key match restores the corresponding cache and counts as a cache hit.
The action can use a partial match when the complete dependency-specific key is unavailable.
Restore keys provide progressively broader fallback prefixes and are evaluated in the order written.
A cache hit means the cached files are restored to the configured path.
After a successful miss, the action saves the selected path under the newly computed key.
gotchas: A cache is saved only after the job completes successfully; a failed job does not create the new cache.
A restore-key fallback can restore an older partial cache, so the install step must still reconcile dependencies.
Only files under path are cached, so choose the package-manager cache directory rather than assuming installed dependencies are included.

Data & performance::Job outputs.summary: Return named values from one GitHub Actions job so dependent jobs can consume them. Map job outputs to step outputs, declare the dependency with needs, and read values through the needs context.
Data & performance::Job outputs.explanation: Define named values under a job's outputs by mapping them to step outputs. A downstream job must depend on the producing job with needs, then it can read each value through needs.<job_id>.outputs.<output_name>.

parameters.name: job_id
parameters.description: The producing job's identifier in the workflow.

parameters.name: output_name
parameters.description: The name assigned to a value in the producing job's outputs map.

Data & performance::Job outputs.returns: A string value for each named job output, available to dependent downstream jobs.

example.title: Pass a version between jobs
example.code:
name: Job outputs
on: push
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      version: ${{ steps.version.outputs.value }}
    steps:
      - id: version
        run: echo "value=1.2.3" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
  publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: build
    steps:
      - env:
          VERSION: ${{ needs.build.outputs.version }}
        run: echo "Publishing version $VERSION"
example.explanation: The first job exposes a step output as a job output. The dependent job declares needs and reads that value through the needs context.

useCases.title: Publish build metadata
useCases.scenario: A build job computes a version, digest, or artifact identifier that a later publishing job needs.

useCases.title: Gate a deployment
useCases.scenario: A validation job determines whether a deployment should proceed and exposes that decision to a dependent job.

useCases.title: Share generated configuration
useCases.scenario: A discovery job produces a value used to parameterize later workflow work.

interview.question: How do you pass a value from one job to another?
interview.answer: Declare the values under jobs.<job_id>.outputs and map each one to a step output. A consuming job uses needs to depend on the producer and reads the value with needs.<job_id>.outputs.<output_name>.
interview.followUp: What happens if the consumer does not declare needs? The documented needs context contains outputs from jobs that are direct dependencies, so the consumer should explicitly depend on the producer.

interview.question: What type are GitHub Actions job outputs?
interview.answer: Job outputs are strings. Expressions in those outputs are evaluated on the runner when the producing job reaches the end of its execution.
interview.followUp: How should structured data be handled? Serialize it into a string in the producing step and parse it after reading the output in the dependent job.

interview.question: How does a step output become a job output?
interview.answer: A job output is created by exposing a step output in the producing job's outputs map. In modern workflows, the step can write a name-value pair to GITHUB_OUTPUT, which becomes available through the mapped job output.
interview.followUp: Why use an intermediate step output? The job-level declaration maps the step's value into the job-level interface that dependent jobs can consume.

keyPoints: Job outputs provide a workflow-level way to transfer values between separate jobs.
Any downstream job that declares the producer as a dependency can consume its outputs.
Read a producer's values through the needs context in the dependent job.
The consumer's expression includes the producer job ID and the selected output name.
gotchas: Expressions used in job outputs are evaluated only after the producing job finishes.
Do not use job outputs to transmit secrets; GitHub redacts them instead of sending them to the service.

Data & performance::Matrix builds.sourceTitle: Running variations of jobs in a workflow
Data & performance::Matrix builds.summary: Use a matrix strategy to run one job across combinations of versions, platforms, or other variables. GitHub generates a separate job for each combination.
Data & performance::Matrix builds.explanation: A matrix strategy expands one job definition into separate runs for every combination of values declared under jobs.<job_id>.strategy.matrix. Matrix variables are available through the matrix context, so the same job can select its runner and tool versions for each generated run.

parameters.name: jobs.<job_id>.strategy.matrix
parameters.description: Object containing one or more matrix variables, each mapped to an array of values.

parameters.name: jobs.<job_id>.strategy.matrix.include
parameters.description: List of objects used to add or expand configurations.

parameters.name: jobs.<job_id>.strategy.matrix.exclude
parameters.description: List of configurations to omit from the generated matrix.

Data & performance::Matrix builds.returns: A set of generated job runs, one for each matrix configuration.

example.title: Test across Node.js versions and operating systems
example.code:
name: Matrix tests
on: push
jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node: [20, 22]
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
      - run: npm test
example.explanation: This workflow creates one test job for every Node.js and operating-system combination.

useCases.title: Version compatibility testing
useCases.scenario: Run tests against several language or runtime versions.

useCases.title: Cross-platform validation
useCases.scenario: Execute the same checks on Linux, Windows, and macOS runners.

useCases.title: Selective configuration coverage
useCases.scenario: Add or omit exceptional configurations without duplicating a job.

interview.question: How does a matrix create jobs?
interview.answer: Define the dimensions under jobs.<job_id>.strategy.matrix, with each variable assigned an array of values. GitHub creates a job for every possible combination of those values.
interview.followUp: How would you add a configuration that is not produced by the Cartesian product? Use strategy.matrix.include with an object describing the additional configuration.

interview.question: How are matrix values consumed?
interview.answer: Reference a matrix variable with the matrix context, such as ${{ matrix.os }} or ${{ matrix.version }}. This lets fields such as runs-on and action inputs vary for each generated job.
interview.followUp: How can a matrix be reduced to selected combinations? Add objects under strategy.matrix.exclude for the configurations to omit.

interview.question: What are the scaling and concurrency considerations?
interview.answer: A matrix can contain multiple variables, creating a multi-dimensional set of configurations. Every possible combination becomes a separate job, subject to the documented limit of 256 jobs per workflow run.
interview.followUp: How can execution concurrency be bounded? Configure jobs.<job_id>.strategy.max-parallel to set the maximum number of matrix jobs running simultaneously.

keyPoints: A matrix turns one reusable job definition into multiple generated job runs.
Declare each matrix dimension as a variable whose value is an array.
With several dimensions, GitHub runs the job for every Cartesian-product combination.
Declared dimensions are exposed as properties of the matrix context for expressions.
Use include to enrich generated combinations or append custom configurations.
gotchas: A single workflow run can create at most 256 matrix jobs, including jobs on both GitHub-hosted and self-hosted runners.
Use include as a list of objects when adding custom configurations or expanding existing combinations.
Use exclude to remove particular combinations from the generated set.

Data & performance::Service containers.summary: Run Docker-based databases, caches, web services, and other dependencies alongside a GitHub Actions job. Declare them under `services`; GitHub starts fresh containers for the job and removes them afterward.
Data & performance::Service containers.explanation: A service container is a Docker container declared under a job's services mapping. GitHub starts a fresh container for each configured service, makes it available to that job's steps, and removes it when the job finishes. Use the service label as the hostname for container jobs; when steps run directly on the runner, map ports and connect through localhost.

parameters.name: services
parameters.description: Mapping of service labels to Docker container configuration for a job.

parameters.name: image
parameters.description: Docker image to run for a service.

parameters.name: env
parameters.description: Environment variables passed to the service container.

parameters.name: ports
parameters.description: Port mappings between the service container and Docker host.

Data & performance::Service containers.returns: A running service container available to steps in the same job until that job completes.

example.title: PostgreSQL service for integration tests
example.code:
name: Integration tests

on: [push]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready
          --health-interval 10s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 5
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm test
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/postgres
example.explanation: This job starts PostgreSQL as a service, maps its port to the runner, waits for its health check, and runs integration tests against it.

useCases.title: Test against PostgreSQL or another database
useCases.scenario: Integration tests need a real relational database.

useCases.title: Run a cache service
useCases.scenario: Application tests depend on an in-memory data store.

useCases.title: Provide a web service or broker
useCases.scenario: A workflow needs an HTTP or messaging dependency.

keyPoints: Service containers let a job run supporting databases, web services, caches, or similar dependencies alongside its steps.
Declare services separately for each job that needs them.
Each configured service gets a new Docker container and is removed after the job completes.
All steps in the job can communicate with its declared service containers.
Use the services keyword under a job to configure containers.
Use ports to expose a service container port on the Docker host.
gotchas: Service containers cannot be created or used inside a composite action.
Jobs using service containers require a Linux runner.

Reuse & environments::Composite actions.sourceTitle: Creating a composite action - GitHub Docs
Reuse & environments::Composite actions.summary: Composite actions package multiple workflow steps behind one action. Store the definition in action.yml, then invoke it as one step from multiple workflows.
Reuse & environments::Composite actions.explanation: A composite action is defined by an action.yml file and groups several workflow steps behind one action invocation. The grouped steps can include shell commands and other actions, allowing the same sequence to be called from multiple workflows; a local action is referenced with the folder path containing its metadata file.

example.title: Calling a local composite action
example.code:
name: Use local composite action
on: push
jobs:
  greet:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: ./.github/actions/hello-world-composite-action
        with:
          who-to-greet: Mona
example.explanation: This workflow checks out the repository and invokes a composite action stored at the recommended local path.

useCases.title: Share repeated commands
useCases.scenario: Several workflows need the same sequence of shell commands.

useCases.title: Organize a local action
useCases.scenario: A repository wants its automation helper kept with the workflows that use it.

useCases.title: Simplify workflow steps
useCases.scenario: A workflow should expose several implementation steps as one callable unit.

interview.question: What problem do composite actions solve?
interview.answer: A composite action bundles multiple workflow steps into one callable action. This lets workflows invoke the bundle as a single step and reuse the same sequence across workflows.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid confusing this with a reusable workflow? A reusable workflow runs a complete workflow from another workflow, whereas a composite action packages steps into one action.

interview.question: How do you create and call a repository-local composite action?
interview.answer: Create an action.yml file in the action directory and define the metadata and steps there. A workflow then references that directory with uses.
interview.followUp: Where is a convenient location for a repository-local action? The documentation recommends placing it under .github/actions for organization.

interview.question: What can a composite action contain?
interview.answer: A composite action can combine multiple workflow steps, including multiple run commands, and expose them through one action invocation. The workflow still executes the bundled commands as part of the calling job.
interview.followUp: When should a reusable workflow be considered instead? Use one when the reusable unit should be a complete workflow rather than a set of steps.

keyPoints: A composite action groups a sequence of workflow steps behind one action interface.
The same grouped action can be invoked as one step from multiple workflows.
The action is described by an action.yml metadata file placed in its directory.
For repository-local actions, .github/actions is the recommended organizational location.
Composite actions are useful for packaging repeated shell commands into a reusable action.
gotchas: For an action in the same repository, the uses value must point to the directory containing action.yml using a relative path.
Composite actions do not have to live in a separate public repository; they can be kept alongside the workflows that use them.

Reuse & environments::Deployment jobs.summary: Deployment jobs sequence workflow work with `needs` and target a named environment with `environment`. Dependencies enforce ordering, while environments can gate execution with approvals and protection rules and control access to deployment secrets.
Reuse & environments::Deployment jobs.explanation: A workflow job can declare dependencies on other jobs with `needs`. Jobs without dependencies run concurrently; a dependent job waits for the prerequisite to finish. A deployment job can also reference an environment, causing its configured protection rules to be checked before the job starts and controlling when its environment secrets become available.

parameters.name: jobs.<job_id>
parameters.description: Job identifiers under `jobs`; each job may use `needs` for dependencies and `environment` for a deployment target.

parameters.name: jobs.<job_id>.needs
parameters.description: Job identifier or identifiers that must complete before this job runs.

parameters.name: jobs.<job_id>.environment
parameters.description: Environment name, or an object containing `name`, optional `url`, and optional `deployment`.

example.title: Sequential build, test, and deployment
example.code:
name: Build, test, and deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run build

  test:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

  deploy:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - run: echo "Deploying to production"
example.explanation: The workflow makes testing wait for a successful build, then makes deployment wait for testing. The production environment can add approval, branch, protection-rule, and secret controls.

useCases.title: Sequential delivery stages
useCases.scenario: A pipeline should build first, test the result second, and deploy only after tests finish.

useCases.title: Gated production deployment
useCases.scenario: Production releases require human approval or branch restrictions.

useCases.title: Environment-aware deployment tracking
useCases.scenario: A workflow must expose which target received a deployment.

useCases.title: Staging and production targets
useCases.scenario: Separate environments need different protection rules and secrets.

interview.question: How do you sequence jobs in GitHub Actions?
interview.answer: Use `needs` on the downstream job, such as `needs: build`. Jobs have no dependencies by default and otherwise run in parallel; a dependent job waits for the prerequisite to complete.
interview.followUp: How would you add a production gate? Assign `environment: production` to the deployment job and configure protection rules, such as required reviewers, for that environment.

interview.question: How do environments affect a deployment job?
interview.answer: Put `environment` under the deployment job, for example `environment: production`. The job is subject to that environment's configured rules, and environment secrets become available only after those rules pass.
interview.followUp: What happens if the environment has required reviewers? The job waits for approval before starting.

interview.question: What does an environment provide for deployments?
interview.answer: A job can reference one environment. Referencing it associates the workflow job with that deployment target and enables environment controls such as approvals, branch restrictions, deployment protection rules, and environment secrets.
interview.followUp: Can a job use multiple environments directly? No; each job can reference only a single environment, so separate jobs are needed for distinct environment targets.

keyPoints: Use `needs` to make a later job wait for an earlier job, which lets a workflow express build-to-test-to-deploy sequencing.
Jobs are isolated execution units and receive their own runner or container rather than sharing one execution context automatically.
Attach one deployment target to a job through its `environment` property, such as `production`, `staging`, or `development`.
Configure an environment to pause a deployment for reviewer approval before the job proceeds.
Environment rules can limit eligible branches, helping prevent deployments from unapproved branch sources.
Referencing an environment records the target in the repository's deployment view, making the deployment target visible.
gotchas: Do not assume job order from YAML placement; declare every required dependency explicitly with `needs`.
An environment can delay deployment before a runner is assigned, so required reviewers and other protection rules must be satisfied first.
Environment secrets are unavailable until protection rules pass; do not expect them during the approval-gated portion of the job.

Reuse & environments::Environments.summary: Use a job-level environment to gate deployments with protection rules such as required reviewers. Secrets stored in that environment are available only to referencing jobs, and only after required approval.
Reuse & environments::Environments.explanation: A job opts into an environment with the environment key. GitHub evaluates that environment's protection rules, such as required reviewers, before the job proceeds; environment secrets are withheld until approval and can then be referenced through the secrets context.

parameters.name: environment
parameters.description: The environment name targeted by the job; it is declared with the job-level environment key.

example.title: Protected deployment job
example.code:
name: Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: ./deploy.sh "$API_TOKEN"
        env:
          API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.PRODUCTION_TOKEN }}
example.explanation: This job targets the production environment, so configured protection rules must pass before the job runs and its environment secret becomes available.

useCases.title: Production approval gate
useCases.scenario: A production deployment should pause until an operations owner approves it.

useCases.title: Environment-scoped credential
useCases.scenario: A deployment needs a credential that must not be exposed to unrelated jobs.

useCases.title: Separation of duties
useCases.scenario: The deployment initiator must not be able to approve their own release.

interview.question: How do you gate a deployment job with an approval?
interview.answer: Set environment on the job, for example environment: production. The job then must satisfy that environment's protection rules before it proceeds, and its environment secrets are unavailable until approval.
interview.followUp: What is the security effect of approval? The job cannot access environment secrets until a required reviewer approves it.

interview.question: How do environment-scoped secrets behave?
interview.answer: Store the credential as an environment secret and reference it through the secrets context. Only jobs that reference that environment can receive the secret, and approval is required first when the environment has that rule.
interview.followUp: How is this different from a repository secret? An environment secret is scoped to jobs referencing its environment and can be protected by environment approval.

interview.question: What constraints apply to required reviewers?
interview.answer: Required reviewers can be users or teams, with at most six configured reviewers. The reviewers need at least read access to the repository, and one configured reviewer can approve the job.
interview.followUp: How can a team prevent the deploy initiator from approving? Enable the environment's prevent-self-review setting.

keyPoints: Configure required reviewers on an environment to pause jobs that target it until an authorized person or team approves.
An environment secret is scoped to jobs that explicitly declare the corresponding environment.
Approval controls both deployment progression and when the job can access protected environment secrets.
An environment can have no more than six required users or teams.
Every configured reviewer needs at least repository read permission.
Environment settings can prevent the person who initiated a deployment from approving it.
gotchas: Approval is not required from every configured reviewer; a single required reviewer is sufficient.
Enable prevention of self-reviews when the person who starts a deployment must not approve it.
On GitHub Free, environment secrets do not apply to private or internal repositories.

Reuse & environments::Reusable workflows.summary: Reusable workflows let one workflow call another through a job-level `uses` reference. The called workflow declares typed inputs and named secrets with `workflow_call`, while the caller supplies them with `with` and `secrets`.
Reuse & environments::Reusable workflows.explanation: A reusable workflow declares an external interface under `on.workflow_call`, defining typed inputs and named secrets. A caller invokes the workflow from a job with `uses`, passes inputs through `with`, and passes secrets through `secrets`; the called workflow reads them through the `inputs` and `secrets` contexts.
Reuse & environments::Reusable workflows.syntax:
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      <name>:
        required: <true|false>
        type: <boolean|number|string>
    secrets:
      <name>:
        required: <true|false>
jobs:
  <job_id>:
    uses: <owner>/<repo>/.github/workflows/<workflow>.yml@<ref>
    with:
      <input-name>: <value>
    secrets:
      <secret-name>: ${{ secrets.<caller-secret> }}

parameters.name: inputs
parameters.description: Input declarations under `on.workflow_call.inputs`, including `required` and `type` such as string, boolean, or number.

parameters.name: secrets
parameters.description: Secret declarations under `on.workflow_call.secrets`, including each secret's `required` setting.

parameters.name: with
parameters.description: Caller job `with` mapping containing values for declared inputs.

parameters.name: secrets
parameters.description: Caller job `secrets` mapping, or `inherit`, containing values for declared secrets.

Reuse & environments::Reusable workflows.returns: A called workflow runs as a job and can use the supplied inputs and secrets; the documentation does not define a separate return value.

example.title: Calling a reusable workflow
example.code:
name: Call reusable workflow
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
jobs:
  call:
    uses: octo-org/example-repo/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@main
    with:
      config-path: .github/config.yml
    secrets:
      personal_access_token: ${{ secrets.PAT }}
example.explanation: A caller job invokes the reusable workflow, supplies its declared input with `with`, and maps a caller secret with `secrets`.

useCases.title: Shared automation
useCases.scenario: Standardize CI or deployment logic across multiple repositories while allowing repository-specific configuration.

useCases.title: Credential handoff
useCases.scenario: Keep credentials out of reusable workflow source and provide only the secrets required by a caller.

useCases.title: Parameterized execution
useCases.scenario: Run the same workflow with different configuration files, modes, or feature flags.

interview.question: How does a reusable workflow declare inputs and secrets?
interview.answer: The called workflow uses `on.workflow_call` to declare its contract. Inputs are defined with names, required status, and a type; secrets are defined by name and required status.
interview.followUp: How does the caller provide them? The caller uses a job-level `uses` reference, then supplies named inputs under `with` and named secrets under `secrets`.

interview.question: How does a caller pass values to a reusable workflow?
interview.answer: A caller invokes a reusable workflow as a job with `uses`, rather than placing `runs-on` or steps in that calling job. Named inputs go under `with`, while named secrets go under `secrets`.
interview.followUp: How can all caller secrets be forwarded? Set the job's `secrets` value to `inherit`, which forwards the caller workflow's secrets to the directly called workflow.

interview.question: How are passed values consumed and validated?
interview.answer: Inside the called workflow, values declared under `workflow_call` are accessed through the `inputs` and `secrets` contexts. For example, a declared input is referenced as `${{ inputs.config-path }}` and a declared secret as `${{ secrets.personal_access_token }}`.
interview.followUp: What validation applies to inputs? The value supplied by the caller must match the declared input type, which can be boolean, number, or string.

keyPoints: Reusable workflows expose a controlled interface so callers can provide configuration and credentials.
Declare the reusable workflow's accepted values beneath `on.workflow_call`.
The calling job maps each input by name under `with`.
Provide individual secrets in the calling job's `secrets` mapping.
Named secret forwarding is configured at the caller job level.
The caller must supply values compatible with the reusable workflow's declared input types.
gotchas: Input values must use the type declared by the reusable workflow: boolean, number, or string.
`secrets: inherit` passes every caller secret, so use it only when the called workflow should receive the complete secret set.

Reuse & environments::Self-hosted runner.summary: Keep untrusted workflow code away from persistent self-hosted runners. Prefer clean GitHub-hosted runners or one-job ephemeral self-hosted runners to reduce compromise and cross-job exposure.
Reuse & environments::Self-hosted runner.explanation: A persistent self-hosted runner may retain modifications made by an earlier job, allowing untrusted workflow code to affect later jobs and potentially access credentials available to the runner. Prefer GitHub-hosted ephemeral machines for untrusted workloads; when self-hosting is necessary, use ephemeral runners that execute one job and are then removed.

example.title: Run trusted code on a fresh hosted runner
example.code:
name: trusted-build
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
example.explanation: A GitHub-hosted runner provides a fresh environment for this build, avoiding reuse of a persistent self-hosted machine.

useCases.title: Isolate untrusted pull-request builds
useCases.scenario: Testing pull requests from contributors or forks

useCases.title: Use one-job ephemeral self-hosted runners
useCases.scenario: Running jobs that require custom hardware or software

useCases.title: Limit runner exposure to secrets
useCases.scenario: Protecting credentials and repository write access

interview.question: Why is a persistent self-hosted runner unsafe for untrusted code?
interview.answer: GitHub-hosted runners are ephemeral, clean virtual machines, while self-hosted runners do not provide that guarantee. Untrusted code can therefore persist changes or compromise a self-hosted environment.
interview.followUp: How can self-hosting reduce this risk? Use ephemeral runners that accept only one job and are then automatically removed, so later jobs receive a clean environment.

interview.question: What runner strategy should be used for untrusted pull requests?
interview.answer: Use GitHub-hosted runners for untrusted workloads when possible. If self-hosting is required, provision ephemeral runners and avoid exposing sensitive credentials to jobs that process untrusted code.
interview.followUp: Why does an ephemeral runner help? GitHub assigns it one job, allowing automation to create a clean system for the next job.

interview.question: Why can private repositories still expose a self-hosted runner?
interview.answer: A private or internal repository is not automatically safe. Someone who can fork it and open a pull request may be able to compromise the runner, including accessing secrets and the `GITHUB_TOKEN`.
interview.followUp: What must be assessed next? Review who can contribute through forks and what secrets and token permissions the workflow makes available.

keyPoints: GitHub-hosted runners start from clean, temporary virtual machines, limiting persistence between jobs.
Untrusted workflow code can leave a persistent self-hosted runner compromised for subsequent jobs.
Private and internal repositories still require caution because fork-based pull requests can run untrusted code.
gotchas: Public repositories are especially risky because pull requests from arbitrary users can execute code that compromises a persistent self-hosted runner.
A compromised runner can expose secrets and the token, whose permissions may allow repository writes.
Environment protections and required reviews do not make a self-hosted runner isolated from the workflow that runs there.

Reuse & environments::Variables and secr.summary: Separate reusable, non-sensitive configuration into variables and keep credentials in secrets. Choose organization, repository, environment, or workflow scope according to who needs the value.
Reuse & environments::Variables and secr.explanation: Use variables for reusable, non-sensitive configuration and secrets for sensitive values. Define them at organization, repository, or environment scope, then explicitly expose each value through the vars or secrets context where a workflow or action needs it.

example.title: Use scoped configuration and credentials
example.code:
name: Deploy
on: workflow_dispatch

jobs:
  deploy:
    environment: production
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      API_URL: ${{ vars.API_URL }}
    steps:
      - run: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}" "$API_URL/health"
example.explanation: A job selects the production environment, reads non-sensitive configuration through vars, and supplies a secret only where the command needs it.

useCases.title: Shared build configuration
useCases.scenario: A compiler flag or server name is reused across several workflows.

useCases.title: Environment-specific settings
useCases.scenario: A deployment differs between staging and production.

useCases.title: Credential injection
useCases.scenario: A deployment action needs a token without exposing it as ordinary configuration.

interview.question: When should GitHub Actions variables be used instead of secrets?
interview.answer: Use variables for non-sensitive configuration such as server names or compiler flags, and secrets for sensitive information. Variables can be defined at organization, repository, or environment scope and referenced through vars; secrets must be explicitly included in the workflow.
interview.followUp: What happens if a reusable workflow needs a secret? The caller must pass it explicitly, because secrets are not automatically forwarded.

interview.question: How do you choose the scope for a configuration value?
interview.answer: Choose the narrowest scope that matches the reuse requirement. A single workflow can use env, while configuration shared across workflows belongs at organization, repository, or environment level; an environment job can then consume environment-specific values.
interview.followUp: Why avoid putting credentials in vars? Variables render unmasked by default, so sensitive data belongs in secrets.

interview.question: How should a workflow expose a secret to an action?
interview.answer: A job can select an environment and reference non-sensitive configuration with vars while exposing a credential through secrets. The secret is available to an action when supplied as an input or environment variable in the workflow.
interview.followUp: Can the secret appear directly in an if expression? No; map it to a job-level environment variable and test that variable instead.

keyPoints: Use variables for reusable settings that are not confidential, such as compiler flags, usernames, or server names.
Shared configuration can live at organization, repository, or environment scope, letting you match visibility to the workflows that need it.
For configuration limited to one workflow, declare it with the workflow file's env key instead of creating a broader configuration variable.
gotchas: Do not put passwords or other sensitive values in variables: variables are unmasked in build output, so use secrets instead.
A secret cannot be used directly in an if condition; first map it to a job-level environment variable if conditional logic requires it.
When calling a reusable workflow, pass required secrets explicitly rather than assuming the called workflow can access them.

Security::Dependency review.summary: Use GitHub’s dependency review action in pull-request workflows to detect vulnerable dependency versions. Require its check to block merges when a pull request introduces a vulnerable dependency.
Security::Dependency review.explanation: The action compares dependency changes in a pull request with known vulnerability data. It fails its check when vulnerable packages are found; configuring that check as a required status check prevents the pull request from merging until the dependency issue is addressed.

parameters.name: fail-on-severity
parameters.description: Minimum vulnerability severity that makes the action fail, such as moderate.

Security::Dependency review.returns: The action reports dependency changes and vulnerability findings through the workflow check; the check fails when its configured failure condition is met.

example.title: Fail a pull request for moderate-or-higher vulnerabilities
example.code:
name: Dependency review

on:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  dependency-review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Dependency Review
        uses: actions/dependency-review-action@v4
        with:
          fail-on-severity: moderate
example.explanation: This workflow runs the dependency review action for pull requests and fails when a newly introduced vulnerability is at least moderate severity.

useCases.title: Review dependency updates
useCases.scenario: A pull request changes a package manifest or lockfile and may introduce a known vulnerable version.

useCases.title: Enforce a merge gate
useCases.scenario: A repository wants vulnerability findings to prevent merging until they are resolved.

useCases.title: Set a severity threshold
useCases.scenario: A team wants only moderate-or-higher findings to fail CI.

interview.question: What does the dependency review action inspect, and what happens when it finds a vulnerable package?
interview.answer: The dependency review action examines package-version changes in pull requests and reports known vulnerabilities in newly introduced dependency versions. Its check fails by default when it finds vulnerable packages.
interview.followUp: How do you turn that failure into a merge block? Require the dependency review check as a branch-protection status check.

interview.question: How can a workflow choose the vulnerability severity that causes failure?
interview.answer: Add actions/dependency-review-action@v4 to a pull-request workflow. Set fail-on-severity to a threshold such as moderate when failures should apply only at that severity or above.
interview.followUp: What is the operational consequence of raising the threshold? Lower-severity findings no longer cause the configured action check to fail.

interview.question: What guidance applies when dependency submission actions are also used?
interview.answer: Dependency review can be paired with dependency submission actions to supply dependency information. Those submission actions should run in the same workflow, with ordering controlled so review executes after the necessary dependency data is available.
interview.followUp: Why does workflow placement matter? The documentation says using the same workflow ensures dependency review will always work.

keyPoints: Install the action in a repository workflow triggered by pull requests to enforce review of dependency changes.
The scan focuses on dependency versions added or changed by the pull request, rather than every dependency in the repository.
Without a severity override, finding any vulnerable package causes the action check to fail.
Configure the workflow check as required in repository merge protections to prevent vulnerable dependency changes from merging.
A newly added dependency with known vulnerability data produces an error in the pull-request workflow.
gotchas: The action alone does not necessarily prevent merging: the repository must require the dependency review check to pass.
If dependency data is produced by submission actions, place those actions in the same workflow so review runs with the dependency information it needs.

Security::GITHUB_TOKEN permissions.summary: Configure GITHUB_TOKEN with the permissions key and grant only the minimum access a workflow needs. Prefer read access for repository contents, then add narrowly scoped permissions where required.
Security::GITHUB_TOKEN permissions.explanation: GitHub Actions lets you control the automatically provided GITHUB_TOKEN with the workflow or job-level permissions key. Start with only the access needed—normally read access for repository contents—and add narrowly scoped permissions when a job requires them.

parameters.name: permission
parameters.description: Permission scope such as contents, actions, checks, or security-events.

Security::GITHUB_TOKEN permissions.returns: No value; the permissions declaration configures the GITHUB_TOKEN available to workflow jobs.

example.title: Read-only GITHUB_TOKEN
example.code:
name: Read-only workflow
on: push
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: git status
example.explanation: This workflow grants repository-content read access to every job and does not grant write access.

useCases.title: Read-only CI
useCases.scenario: A workflow only checks out code, runs tests, or reads repository metadata.

useCases.title: Targeted write access
useCases.scenario: One job publishes a release, writes a deployment status, or uploads security results.

useCases.title: Per-job isolation
useCases.scenario: Different jobs have different trust levels or responsibilities.

interview.question: How can a workflow control GITHUB_TOKEN access?
interview.answer: Use the permissions key at workflow scope to affect all jobs, or inside a job to limit the token used by that job. Each permission accepts read, write, or none where supported.
interview.followUp: What happens to unspecified permissions when one is declared? They become none, so explicitly list all required scopes.

interview.question: How should you choose permission levels?
interview.answer: Set contents to read for a read-only workflow, and grant write only to the specific permission and job that must modify GitHub resources. This follows the minimum-required-access principle.
interview.followUp: Why is read-only a safer default? It reduces what compromised or untrusted workflow code can do with the token.

interview.question: What is the difference between workflow-level and job-level permissions?
interview.answer: The permissions key can be placed at the top level or within an individual job. Job-level configuration applies to actions and run commands in that job that use GITHUB_TOKEN.
interview.followUp: When is job-level configuration preferable? Use it when only one job needs elevated access and other jobs should remain restricted.

keyPoints: Use the permissions key to replace or refine the token permissions supplied by default.
Apply least privilege: grant each workflow only the scopes it genuinely needs.
Put permissions at workflow level for a shared policy or at job level for narrower access.
Permission scopes use read, write, or none, depending on whether that access level is supported.
The read-all shorthand grants read access across all available permission scopes.
gotchas: Declaring one permission explicitly disables every other permission not listed, so include every scope the workflow or job needs.
A write grant also provides read access for that permission; use read when mutation is unnecessary.

Security::OIDC to cloud providers.sourceTitle: Configuring OpenID Connect in cloud providers
Security::OIDC to cloud providers.summary: GitHub Actions can use OIDC to obtain short-lived cloud access without storing long-lived credentials as GitHub secrets. Configure cloud federation, grant id-token: write, and exchange the workflow JWT with the provider's official login action.
Security::OIDC to cloud providers.explanation: First configure the cloud provider to trust GitHub's OIDC identity as a federated identity. Then grant the workflow id-token: write permission and use the provider's official login action, which obtains GitHub's JWT and exchanges it for a cloud access token.
Security::OIDC to cloud providers.returns: A short-lived cloud access token issued by the cloud provider.

example.title: OIDC-based cloud authentication
example.code:
name: Deploy
on: push
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Authenticate to cloud
        uses: <cloud-provider-login-action>@<version>
        with:
          audience: <cloud-provider-audience>
          role: <cloud-role>
      - run: ./deploy.sh
example.explanation: Replace the placeholder login action and inputs with the official action and configuration for your cloud provider.

useCases.title: Keyless deployments
useCases.scenario: A deployment workflow needs access to AWS, Azure, GCP, or another OIDC-capable provider without storing static cloud keys.

useCases.title: Short-lived cloud access
useCases.scenario: A workflow must receive temporary authorization for cloud resources during a deployment run.

useCases.title: Federated workload identity
useCases.scenario: An organization wants cloud trust policies to identify approved GitHub workflows rather than distribute reusable secrets.

interview.question: How does GitHub Actions authenticate to a cloud provider without stored keys?
interview.answer: Configure a trust relationship in the cloud provider, grant the job id-token: write, and invoke the provider's official login action. That action exchanges GitHub's OIDC JWT for a cloud access token.
interview.followUp: What prevents every repository from assuming the cloud role? Configure the cloud provider's trust policy to restrict which GitHub workflows or identities may request the role.

interview.question: What does OIDC exchange provide to the workflow?
interview.answer: The workflow requests a short-lived OIDC token from GitHub, and the cloud provider validates it through the configured federated trust. The provider then returns temporary access credentials or a cloud access token.
interview.followUp: Why prefer this over a long-lived secret? The token is short-lived and avoids storing a reusable private credential in GitHub.

interview.question: What workflow changes are required to enable OIDC?
interview.answer: The workflow YAML needs a permissions setting containing id-token: write. It also needs a cloud login action or custom script that fetches the OIDC token and presents it to the provider.
interview.followUp: Where should authorization boundaries be enforced? Enforce them in the cloud provider's trust configuration and role permissions, not only in workflow steps.

keyPoints: OIDC replaces persistent GitHub credentials with an identity token issued for the workflow.
The recommended workflow pattern delegates token exchange to the cloud provider's official action.
Enable the workflow's OIDC token permission at the job or workflow level.
Cloud federation is a prerequisite: the provider must trust GitHub's OIDC issuer.
Every deployment should explicitly obtain and submit an OIDC token through a login action or script.
gotchas: Without id-token: write, GitHub cannot issue the workflow's OIDC JWT.
Authentication must occur for each deployment; do not assume a previously obtained token is reusable.
Cloud-side federation must be configured before the workflow can exchange its token.

Security::Pinning actions.summary: Pin third-party GitHub Actions to full commit SHAs instead of moving tags. This makes the selected action revision immutable and reduces supply-chain risk from later repository changes.
Security::Pinning actions.explanation: A workflow selects an action with OWNER/REPOSITORY@REFERENCE. Replace a mutable tag such as v1 with the action repository's full commit SHA. That fixes execution to the reviewed revision and reduces the chance that later repository changes introduce a backdoor. Confirm that the SHA belongs to the action's repository rather than a fork.

parameters.name: action reference
parameters.description: Action repository owner and repository name, followed by a tag or full commit SHA.

example.title: Pin an action to a commit
example.code:
name: CI
on: push
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@f43a0e5ff2bd294095638e18286ca9a3d1956744
      - run: npm test
example.explanation: The workflow uses the complete commit SHA for checkout, so the referenced action resolves to the reviewed immutable revision.

useCases.title: Reproducible CI
useCases.scenario: A production workflow must keep running the exact action code that was reviewed.

useCases.title: Third-party dependency hardening
useCases.scenario: A repository consumes actions maintained outside the organization.

useCases.title: Policy enforcement
useCases.scenario: An organization wants workflows to reject mutable action references.

interview.question: How do you pin a third-party action?
interview.answer: Use the action reference form OWNER/REPOSITORY@REFERENCE, with REFERENCE set to the complete commit SHA. This identifies one exact Git object instead of following a moving tag.
interview.followUp: Why does this improve supply-chain security? An attacker who changes the action repository cannot change the already selected revision without producing a valid SHA-1 collision.

interview.question: Why prefer a full-length SHA over a version tag?
interview.answer: A full-length commit SHA is the only documented way to use an action as an immutable release. A tag is easier to read, but it can later point to different code.
interview.followUp: When might a tag still be used? Only when the action creator is trusted and the convenience trade-off is acceptable.

interview.question: What should you verify before pinning a SHA?
interview.answer: The SHA must be checked against the action's own repository, not a fork. Otherwise the workflow may execute code from an unintended source even though the reference is a commit.
interview.followUp: What additional signal can help when choosing a tag? GitHub's Verified creator badge indicates that the author's identity has been verified, but it does not remove tag mutability.

keyPoints: Use a full-length commit SHA when the workflow must execute an immutable action release.
A fixed SHA limits the impact of later malicious changes to the action repository.
Changing the code behind an already selected SHA would require a valid Git-object SHA-1 collision.
Tags are more convenient for maintenance, but commit pinning provides stronger protection.
If using a tag, the Marketplace Verified creator badge is one signal when evaluating the publisher.
gotchas: A commit-looking reference from a fork is not an adequate substitute; verify the SHA's repository of origin.
Trusting an author does not make tag references immutable; tags may be moved or deleted.

Security::pull_request_target risks.summary: pull_request_target runs with the base repository's privileges, including its GITHUB_TOKEN and secrets. Never use that privileged context to execute untrusted pull-request code, because a malicious fork can compromise the repository.
Security::pull_request_target risks.explanation: The pull_request_target event runs in the context of the base repository, so its jobs can receive the base repository's GITHUB_TOKEN and repository or organization secrets. A malicious pull request can exploit this privilege if the workflow checks out, downloads, builds, tests, or otherwise executes pull-request content. Keep untrusted files as data only, or use a nonprivileged design for running their code.

example.title: Inspect pull-request metadata safely
example.code:
name: Safe privileged workflow
on:
  pull_request_target:
    types: [opened, synchronize]
jobs:
  inspect:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Inspect metadata only
        run: echo "PR #${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}"
example.explanation: This workflow uses the privileged trigger without checking out, building, or executing files from the pull request.

useCases.title: Privileged metadata inspection
useCases.scenario: Read pull-request metadata or inspect untrusted content without executing it.

useCases.title: Controlled privileged automation
useCases.scenario: Perform a trusted operation that genuinely requires the base repository's token or secrets.

keyPoints: The trigger runs with elevated privileges and gives the job the base repository's token and access to repository and organization secrets.
Secrets available to the privileged job can be exposed if attacker-controlled pull-request code runs.
Checking out the pull request head or merge commit is a risky pattern when subsequent steps execute it.
Build, test, and execution steps turn untrusted checkout content into a potential repository compromise.
Using git fetch, gh pr checkout, or fork artifacts does not make untrusted code safe.
If this trigger is necessary, treat checked-out content strictly as data and never execute it.
gotchas: Checking out untrusted pull-request code is not safe by itself when a later step executes the working tree.
A forked pull request can carry malicious commands in build scripts, tests, dependencies, or configuration.
Do not override the default behavior to run code supplied by the fork.
Downloading pull-request code through methods other than checkout is equally dangerous if the result is executed.

Security::Secret handling.summary: GitHub Actions masks secrets printed in workflow logs, but masking is limited to secrets used by the current job and is not guaranteed for transformed values. Avoid intentional printing, mask other sensitive values, and rotate credentials exposed in unredacted logs.
Security::Secret handling.explanation: GitHub Actions redacts secrets used in a job when they appear in workflow logs, but transformed or otherwise sensitive values are not automatically safe. Avoid deliberate printing, mask non-secret sensitive values before output, and delete logs and rotate a secret if an unredacted value appears.

example.title: Mask a generated sensitive value
example.code:
name: Mask generated value
on: workflow_dispatch
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Generate and mask
        shell: bash
        run: |
          value="generated-sensitive-value"
          echo "::add-mask::$value"
          echo "value=$value" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
example.explanation: The value is generated without first printing it, registered with the runner using add-mask, and then made available through GITHUB_OUTPUT.

useCases.title: Protect generated values
useCases.scenario: A workflow creates a token, certificate, or other sensitive value during a job and must pass it to a later step without exposing it in logs.

useCases.title: Mask non-secret sensitive data
useCases.scenario: A workflow handles sensitive input that is not stored as a GitHub secret.

useCases.title: Safely consume workflow secrets
useCases.scenario: A workflow needs to use credentials while preventing accidental disclosure through command output.

useCases.title: Respond to log exposure
useCases.scenario: A security review finds a credential visible in a workflow run log.

interview.question: When does GitHub Actions redact a secret?
interview.answer: GitHub Actions automatically redacts GitHub secrets printed to workflow logs when the secret was used in the job and is accessible to its runner. This protection is not guaranteed for transformed values.
interview.followUp: How would you protect a generated token? Generate it without outputting it, issue the add-mask command before any logging, and pass it using GITHUB_OUTPUT.

interview.question: How do you mask non-secret sensitive data?
interview.answer: Use the workflow command ::add-mask::VALUE for sensitive data that is not already a GitHub secret. Masking causes the value to be treated as a secret and redacted by the runner.
interview.followUp: What ordering is required? Register the mask before outputting the value or using it in another workflow command.

interview.question: Why should structured data be avoided as a secret value?
interview.answer: Avoid structured secret values such as JSON or encoded Git blobs because their contents may not be redacted correctly. Prefer separate secrets for individual sensitive values.
interview.followUp: What should happen after exposure? Delete the workflow log and rotate the affected secret.

keyPoints: Secrets used by a job are automatically redacted when they reach that job's workflow log.
Use add-mask for sensitive values that were not stored in GitHub's secret store.
After masking, the runner treats the value as secret material and removes it from log output.
Store simple individual values rather than structured blobs to improve reliable redaction.
gotchas: Redaction may fail when a secret is transformed, such as by encoding or other value changes; register the transformed value as a secret too.
A runner cannot redact a secret in a job where that secret was not used and accessible.
Do not rely on automatic masking as permission to print secrets.
Treat any unredacted log exposure as a compromise: remove the log and rotate the credential.

Workflow fundamentals::Conditions.sourceTitle: Using conditions to control job execution
Workflow fundamentals::Conditions.summary: Use `if` expressions to run a GitHub Actions job or step only when a condition evaluates to true. Conditions can reference supported contexts and expressions.
Workflow fundamentals::Conditions.explanation: GitHub Actions evaluates an expression assigned to `if` and runs the associated job or step only when the result is true. Conditions can use supported contexts and expressions; job conditions are checked before the job is sent to a runner, while step conditions are evaluated during job execution.

parameters.name: if
parameters.description: Expression evaluated by GitHub Actions; a true result permits the associated job or step to run.

Workflow fundamentals::Conditions.returns: No value; controls whether the associated job or step runs.

example.title: Run a job only on the main branch
example.code:
name: Conditional workflow
on: push
jobs:
  deploy:
    if: ${{ github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Deploying from the default branch"
      - name: Report success
        if: ${{ success() }}
        run: echo "Deployment job is running"
example.explanation: Runs the deploy job only for pushes to the main branch, then conditionally runs the final step when earlier steps have succeeded.

useCases.title: Protect deployments
useCases.scenario: Run deployment jobs only for a specific branch or repository.

useCases.title: Reduce unnecessary work
useCases.scenario: Skip expensive checks unless a relevant condition is met.

useCases.title: Control later steps
useCases.scenario: Run cleanup or reporting steps based on earlier step outcomes.

keyPoints: Use `jobs.<job_id>.if` to gate an entire job.
Conditions can combine supported contexts with GitHub Actions expressions.
GitHub evaluates a job condition before dispatching the job to its runner.
A condition can compare a context property with a literal value.
gotchas: Shell-specific tests cannot be placed in a job-level `if`; put them in a step's `run` script instead.

Workflow fundamentals::Events and trigge.summary: GitHub Actions workflows start when configured events occur, such as pushes, pull requests, schedules, manual dispatches, or another workflow's run. The `on` key selects events and can narrow them with filters or activity types.
Workflow fundamentals::Events and trigge.explanation: A workflow trigger is an event that starts a workflow. Declare one or more events under the top-level `on` key, optionally narrowing them with filters, activity types, schedules, or inputs; use `workflow_dispatch` for manual runs and `workflow_run` to react to another workflow.

parameters.name: on
parameters.description: Top-level workflow trigger declaration; accepts event names and event-specific filters, activity types, schedules, or manual inputs.

Workflow fundamentals::Events and trigge.returns: A workflow run when a configured event occurs or a manual dispatch is requested.

example.title: Multiple workflow triggers
example.code:
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  schedule:
    - cron: '30 5 * * 1'
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "Triggered workflow"
example.explanation: This workflow runs for pushes to main, pull-request activity, a weekly scheduled time, or a manual run started from GitHub.

useCases.title: Continuous integration
useCases.scenario: Run validation for changes entering or landing in a repository.

useCases.title: Scheduled automation
useCases.scenario: Execute maintenance or reporting at recurring times.

useCases.title: Manual operations
useCases.scenario: Let an operator launch a deployment or one-off task.

useCases.title: Workflow chaining
useCases.scenario: Start dependent processing after an upstream workflow completes.

interview.question: What is the purpose of the `on` key in a workflow?
interview.answer: The `on` key defines the events that can start a workflow. Common choices include `push`, `pull_request`, `schedule`, and `workflow_dispatch`; each can also accept event-specific configuration such as branch filters or cron entries.
interview.followUp: How would you restrict a push workflow to one branch? Add a `branches` filter beneath `push`, for example `push: { branches: [main] }`.

interview.question: How do manual and workflow-to-workflow triggers differ?
interview.answer: `workflow_dispatch` lets a user start a workflow manually from GitHub. It can also define inputs so the person starting the run supplies values that the workflow can use.
interview.followUp: How can a workflow react after another workflow finishes? Use `workflow_run` and configure the relevant workflow names and activity types.

interview.question: What should you know before using `schedule`?
interview.answer: The `schedule` event uses POSIX cron syntax to run a workflow at planned times. Scheduled workflows run from the default branch, and GitHub may delay them when Actions is under heavy load.
interview.followUp: What alternative should be considered when exact timing is critical? Avoid treating scheduled execution as an exact-time guarantee and design the job to tolerate delayed starts.

keyPoints: A trigger is the event declaration that causes GitHub Actions to create a workflow run.
Events can respond to repository activity, such as pushes and pull requests.
Use `schedule` with one or more cron expressions for recurring execution.
Events that expose activity types can be narrowed to selected actions.

Workflow fundamentals::Expressions and c.summary: GitHub Actions contexts expose workflow, event, job, runner, environment, and step data. Expressions read these values so workflow fields can make decisions and pass dynamic information.
Workflow fundamentals::Expressions and c.explanation: GitHub Actions contexts expose information about the workflow run, environment, jobs, runners, and steps. Expressions use these objects to evaluate conditions and values; for example, the event name comes from the github context, while outputs from an earlier identified step are read through steps.

parameters.name: context
parameters.description: Context object containing workflow, event, job, step, or related execution data.

parameters.name: property
parameters.description: Property or output name selected from a context object.

Workflow fundamentals::Expressions and c.returns: The selected context property or step output value; the expression evaluates to a value usable by the workflow.

example.title: Use event and step contexts in a condition
example.code:
name: Context example
on:
  push:
jobs:
  inspect:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: build
        run: echo "artifact=dist" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - name: Use context data
        if: ${{ github.event_name == 'push' && steps.build.outputs.artifact == 'dist' }}
        run: echo "Running ${{ github.ref }}"
example.explanation: The second step runs only for a push event and after the earlier step has produced the expected output.

useCases.title: Gate execution by event
useCases.scenario: Run a job or step only for a particular trigger, such as push or pull_request.

useCases.title: Inspect event data
useCases.scenario: Use fields from the triggering webhook payload to tailor workflow behavior.

useCases.title: Consume step outputs
useCases.scenario: Pass a generated value from one step into a later step in the same job.

useCases.title: Inspect job state
useCases.scenario: Use current-job metadata when configuring or diagnosing execution.

interview.question: What are GitHub Actions contexts used for?
interview.answer: Contexts are objects that expose workflow data, such as run details, variables, the current job, and completed steps. Expressions read their properties with forms such as github.event_name or steps.build.outputs.result.
interview.followUp: How would you prevent reading an unavailable step output? Give the producing step an id, place the consumer afterward, and ensure the producer executes on the path where the output is needed.

interview.question: How can a workflow branch on its triggering event?
interview.answer: The github context describes the workflow run and includes the event that triggered it. Its event_name property can distinguish triggers such as push from pull_request in an expression.
interview.followUp: How can event-specific payload data be accessed? Use github.event and select the relevant property from that webhook payload.

interview.question: How are outputs from an earlier step consumed?
interview.answer: The steps context provides information about earlier identified steps in the current job. Step outputs are accessed through steps.<step_id>.outputs.<output_name>, allowing later steps to make decisions from generated values.
interview.followUp: Can a later job directly use the steps context from an earlier job? No; expose the value as a job output and consume it through the needs context.

keyPoints: Contexts provide structured data about a run, its runner, jobs, and steps.
Use GitHub Actions expression syntax to read context data in workflow fields that support expressions.
Use github for run metadata and details about the event that started the workflow.
Use job to inspect data associated with the job currently executing.
Use steps to read data from completed, identified steps in the current job.
gotchas: A step must have an id and must already have run before its data can be read from the steps context.

Workflow fundamentals::Jobs and steps.summary: GitHub Actions workflows divide work into jobs, and each job contains ordered steps. Jobs run in parallel by default; use needs to sequence dependent jobs.
