Workflow fundamentals::Jobs and steps.explanation: A workflow groups work into jobs. Each job runs on a selected runner, while its steps execute tasks in order; jobs run concurrently unless needs creates a dependency.
Workflow fundamentals::Jobs and steps.syntax:
jobs:
  <job_id>:
    runs-on: <runner>
    needs: <job_id>
    steps:
      - run: <command>
      - uses: <owner>/<repo>@<ref>

parameters.name: job_id
parameters.description: Job identifier used as the key under jobs.

parameters.name: jobs.<job_id>.runs-on
parameters.description: Runner environment for the job.

parameters.name: jobs.<job_id>.steps
parameters.description: Ordered task list for the job.

parameters.name: jobs.<job_id>.needs
parameters.description: Job identifiers that must complete before this job starts.

example.title: Sequential jobs with ordered steps
example.code:
name: CI
on: [push]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
  deploy:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Deploying"
example.explanation: The test job runs first; deploy waits for it through needs.

useCases.title: Parallel validation
useCases.scenario: Run linting and tests concurrently to shorten feedback time.

useCases.title: Dependency-gated deployment
useCases.scenario: Require tests to pass before publishing or deploying.

useCases.title: Ordered build pipeline
useCases.scenario: Prepare a runner, check out code, install dependencies, and execute commands in a defined order.

interview.question: How do jobs differ from steps?
interview.answer: Jobs are the workflow's units of work and run in parallel by default. A job's runs-on value chooses its runner, and needs can establish a dependency so one job waits for another.
interview.followUp: How would you make deployment wait for tests? Add needs: test to the deployment job, using the test job's identifier.

interview.question: What can a step do, and how does it execute?
interview.answer: A job has a steps sequence. Steps can run commands, setup tasks, or actions, and each step executes in its own process on the runner.
interview.followUp: What consequence does the separate process have? Environment-variable changes do not persist automatically from one step to the next.

interview.question: How do you sequence jobs?
interview.answer: Use jobs.<job_id>.needs to define dependencies between jobs. Without such dependencies, jobs run in parallel by default.
interview.followUp: Can steps in a single job be parallelized with this keyword? No; needs controls job dependencies, while the steps sequence remains within the job.

keyPoints: A workflow can contain multiple jobs, and independent jobs start concurrently unless dependencies are declared.
Set needs on a job to make it wait for the jobs it depends on.
Every job must select its execution environment with runs-on.
Steps are the ordered task list inside a job.
A step can execute shell commands, perform setup, or invoke an action from supported locations.
Each step gets a separate process while sharing the runner's workspace and filesystem.
gotchas: Environment-variable changes made in one step are not automatically available in a later step.
A step may execute a shell command, whereas every action invocation is represented by a step.

Workflow fundamentals::Runners.sourceTitle: Choosing the runner for a job
Workflow fundamentals::Runners.summary: Use `jobs.<job_id>.runs-on` to choose the machine that executes a job. It can target a GitHub-hosted, larger, or self-hosted runner, including by operating-system and architecture labels.
Workflow fundamentals::Runners.explanation: A job's `runs-on` value selects the machine that executes its steps. You can target a GitHub-hosted runner, larger runner, or self-hosted runner; self-hosted jobs use labels to match a suitable machine, commonly starting with `self-hosted` and adding operating-system or architecture labels.

parameters.name: job_id
parameters.description: The job identifier whose execution machine is being selected.

parameters.name: runs-on
parameters.description: A runner image, runner label, label array, or supported expression that selects the execution machine.

Workflow fundamentals::Runners.returns: The selected runner executes the job's workflow steps.

example.title: Select a hosted runner
example.code:
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
example.explanation: This job runs on a GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runner, checks out the repository, installs dependencies, and executes tests.

useCases.title: Hosted continuous integration
useCases.scenario: Run ordinary CI on a maintained Linux image without managing machines.

useCases.title: Specialized self-hosted execution
useCases.scenario: Schedule work requiring custom hardware or software installed on an internal network.

useCases.title: Label-based targeting
useCases.scenario: Ensure a job runs on a particular operating system and processor architecture.

interview.question: How does a workflow choose the machine for a job?
interview.answer: Set `jobs.<job_id>.runs-on` to the runner type or label expression required by the job. A GitHub-hosted runner can be selected with an image such as `ubuntu-latest`, while self-hosted runners are selected using labels.
interview.followUp: How would you target a self-hosted Linux x64 machine with a GPU? Use an array such as `[self-hosted, linux, x64, gpu]`; the runner must have all specified labels.

interview.question: What runner categories can `runs-on` select?
interview.answer: The job can run on a GitHub-hosted runner, a larger runner, or a self-hosted runner. The `runs-on` setting expresses that choice at job level.
interview.followUp: Why might a team choose a self-hosted runner? It can provide specialized hardware, local-network software, or a controlled operating-system environment.

interview.question: How are self-hosted runners targeted?
interview.answer: Self-hosted selection uses runner labels. Labels can represent properties such as the operating system or processor architecture, allowing a job to target a matching runner.
interview.followUp: What does combining labels do? It narrows scheduling to runners carrying the complete requested label set.

keyPoints: Set `jobs.<job_id>.runs-on` to select the machine type for a job.
A job may use a GitHub-hosted runner, larger runner, or self-hosted runner.
Choose a self-hosted machine by assigning its labels to `runs-on`.
Runner labels can encode targeting properties such as operating system and architecture.
An array of labels can target a self-hosted Linux x64 runner equipped with a GPU.
gotchas: When selecting a self-hosted runner with multiple labels, put `self-hosted` first in the label array.

Workflow fundamentals::Workflow files.summary: A workflow is a versioned YAML file that defines when automation starts and what jobs and steps it performs. GitHub can run it for repository events, manually, or on a schedule.
Workflow fundamentals::Workflow files.explanation: A workflow is a version-controlled YAML configuration stored in the repository's .github/workflows directory. GitHub starts it for matching repository events, manual requests, or schedules; each job runs on a runner and is composed of ordered steps that either execute commands or invoke actions.
Workflow fundamentals::Workflow files.syntax:
name: <workflow-name>
on: <event-or-trigger-configuration>
jobs:
  <job_id>:
    runs-on: <runner>
    steps:
      - run: <shell-command>
      - uses: <owner>/<action>@<ref>

parameters.name: on
parameters.description: Repository activity, manual request, or schedule that starts the workflow; configured with on.

parameters.name: jobs
parameters.description: Identifier and configuration for each unit of execution.

parameters.name: jobs.<job_id>
parameters.description: Runner and ordered tasks for a job.

parameters.name: jobs.<job_id>.steps
parameters.description: Command or reusable action executed by a job.

Workflow fundamentals::Workflow files.returns: A workflow run containing one or more jobs executed on runner machines.

example.title: A minimal test workflow
example.code:
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm test
example.explanation: This workflow runs for pushes to main or when started manually. Its test job uses an Ubuntu runner and contains steps that check out the repository and execute the test command.

useCases.title: Run tests when code is pushed or a pull request changes.
useCases.scenario: Continuous integration

useCases.title: Offer an operator-controlled workflow for tasks such as deployment.
useCases.scenario: Manual operations

useCases.title: Run recurring checks or maintenance at defined times.
useCases.scenario: Scheduled maintenance

useCases.title: Combine scripts and published actions into a repeatable job.
useCases.scenario: Reusable automation

interview.question: What does the on key do?
interview.answer: The on key selects the repository events that can start a workflow. It can also represent manual execution or a scheduled trigger.
interview.followUp: How does GitHub find the applicable files? It searches .github/workflows in the commit or ref associated with the event, then runs workflows whose on values match.

interview.question: How are jobs and steps related?
interview.answer: Jobs are the workflow's units of execution. Each job runs on a runner and contains one or more steps.
interview.followUp: What is a step allowed to do? It can execute a script defined in the workflow or run a reusable action.

interview.question: Why are workflow files kept in the repository?
interview.answer: The workflow file is committed as YAML in the repository, allowing its automation definition to be versioned with the code. The file describes triggers, jobs, runners, and steps.
interview.followUp: Where should the file be placed? GitHub searches the repository's .github/workflows directory for workflow files.

keyPoints: Commit workflow definitions alongside source code so changes to automation are reviewable and versioned.
Use on to declare which repository activity starts the workflow.
A workflow must define at least one job, and each job is assigned execution to a runner.
Each job contains an ordered sequence of one or more steps.
Steps support both inline commands and reusable actions.
In addition to repository events, workflows may support manual starts and scheduled execution.
gotchas: For certain events, placing the file only on another branch is insufficient; the workflow must also exist on the default branch.
A file is not run merely because it exists: its on configuration must match the event that occurred.
